home.lead: Search by track, pick the artist and album, then compare pressings by country, year and label. Keep a wishlist and a collection of your own.

help.title: How to search
help.intro: You can start in three ways. Choose one with the Track, Artist or Album buttons in the form.
help.way1: By track name: you remember a song but not the album.
help.way2: By artist: you know who made it and want to browse their albums.
help.way3: By album title: you know which album it is.
help.flow1: Type a track and press Search.
help.flow4: Pick the exact pressing: country, year and label.
help.flow5: Open the release card and add it to your Wishlist or Collection.
help.tip1: The optional artist field narrows a track or album search. It helps when a title is common.
help.tip2: Found nothing? Try the album or artist mode: the track may be listed under a different name.
help.tip4: Coloured, deluxe and special editions are usually under the album’s pressings (“See pressings”).
help.tip5: Releases Discogs has not grouped under an album are in the collapsed section “Other pressings without a master”.
help.tip6: Results can be incomplete. Use “Load more” and “Show more albums” to see further.
help.exampleLine: Example: track “One More Time” by Daft Punk

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.metaDescription: What Vinilium stores about you, why, who else is involved, and how to delete or export your data.
privacy.lead: Vinilium is a free, non-commercial service. This page says plainly what it stores about you and what you can do about it.
privacy.s1P1: Vinilium is run by a private individual as a free, non-commercial hobby project. The operator appears under the project name or nickname “{operator}” and is based in {country}.
privacy.s1P2: The operator named above decides why and how your personal data is used (in data-protection terms, the controller). You can reach the operator at the contact address below; there is no data protection officer. [NEEDS LEGAL REVIEW] Whether a nickname is enough to identify the operator for users in the EU or Norway is not settled.
privacy.s2Intro: Only what the service needs to work:
privacy.s2Account: Your account: your name, your email address, your language, the date you signed up and whether your email address is verified. We need your name and email address to create an account; without them we cannot offer it. For a password account, the password is stored only in hashed form, which we cannot read. If you sign in with Google, we store the link to your Google account and the name and picture address Google provides. We do not store Google’s access tokens.
privacy.s2Sessions: Your sign-ins: a random session identifier, when it expires, and the IP address and browser description (user agent) of the device you signed in from. A sign-in lasts 7 days after your last visit.
privacy.s2Lists: Your lists: the Discogs release numbers you add, which list each is on (Wishlist or Collection), your own notes and condition grades, and dates.
privacy.s2Counters: Request counters: to protect the service from misuse we count requests per IP address and per account for about a minute at a time.
privacy.s2Logs: Server logs: our hosting provider, Vercel, processes technical request data such as your IP address, the time, the address requested and the result, to run and secure the service. Vercel’s documentation says its runtime logs are kept for 1 hour on the free Hobby plan this service uses (longer on paid plans); Vercel may keep other technical records under its own privacy notice.
privacy.s2Emails: Emails: verification and password-reset messages are sent through Brevo, which receives your email address, your name and the content of the message, including its one-time link. Replies to these messages go to our contact address.
privacy.s2bP1: To give you the service you asked for (your account, sign-in, lists, and the verification and reset emails) we rely on the contract between you and us. To keep the service secure and running (request counters, server logs, protection against misuse) we rely on our legitimate interest in doing so. Signing in with Google is your own choice. We do not use your consent as a legal basis, and we do not use your data for marketing.
privacy.s2bP1GoogleOnly: To give you the service you asked for (your account, sign-in and lists) we rely on the contract between you and us. To keep the service secure and running (request counters, server logs, protection against misuse) we rely on our legitimate interest in doing so. Signing in with Google is your own choice. We do not use your consent as a legal basis, and we do not use your data for marketing.
privacy.s3P1: No analytics, no advertising, no tracking of what you do on other sites, no payment data, and no automated decisions about you. We never ask for your Discogs account or password: record details are fetched by our server with the service’s own Discogs credentials.
privacy.s4P1: Record details (titles, artists, covers, track lists) come from Discogs. Our server asks Discogs for them; your browser does not contact Discogs for them. Our server sends the words you search for, and release numbers, to Discogs; Discogs does not receive your name, email address, account or IP address from us. A short-lived cache (at most 6 hours) holds that data for all users together and contains nothing about you; cover images pass through our server and your browser may keep them for the same short time. Links to discogs.com lead to Discogs’ own site, which has its own policies. Vinilium is not affiliated with Discogs.
privacy.s5P1: Cookies we set: the sign-in cookie (better-auth.session_token), which keeps you signed in for up to 7 days and cannot be read by scripts; the language cookie (NEXT_LOCALE), which remembers your language for 1 year; and, only while you sign in with Google, a technical cookie that protects that sign-in and lasts 5 minutes. There are no analytics or advertising cookies, and there is no cookie banner. If that ever changes, this page and a notice will change first.
privacy.s5P3: Your browser may also keep up to two small settings in its local storage (not in cookies): whether you closed the “How to search” help on the search page, and the colour theme you chose (dark, light or system). They stay on your device and are never sent to us.
privacy.s5P2: [NEEDS LEGAL REVIEW] Whether this use of cookies and local storage needs a consent notice for users in the EU and Norway is not settled.
privacy.s6Intro: Services we use to run Vinilium:
privacy.s6Hosting: Vercel: hosting of the website and its server code.
privacy.s6Database: Neon: the database that holds the data above.
privacy.s6Email: Brevo: sending verification and password-reset emails.
privacy.s6Google: Google: signing in with a Google account, if you choose it. Google handles that sign-in under its own privacy policy; we receive your name, email address and picture address.
privacy.s6Discogs: Discogs: the source of record details (see above).
privacy.s6P1: Where these services work: our server code runs in Frankfurt (Germany), but the providers are not all European companies, so your data can be processed outside the EU/EEA. Vercel and Neon (part of Databricks) are US companies; each states in its public documents that it complies with the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework and uses the EU Standard Contractual Clauses. Brevo is a French company that states it relies on the Standard Contractual Clauses, and for the US on the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework, for transfers outside the EEA. Google states that it complies with the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework and uses Standard Contractual Clauses. Discogs receives only the words you search for and release numbers. This is what the providers say in their own documents; we have not audited them.
privacy.s6P1GoogleOnly: Where these services work: our server code runs in Frankfurt (Germany), but the providers are not all European companies, so your data can be processed outside the EU/EEA. Vercel and Neon (part of Databricks) are US companies; each states in its public documents that it complies with the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework and uses the EU Standard Contractual Clauses. Google states that it complies with the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework and uses Standard Contractual Clauses. Discogs receives only the words you search for and release numbers. This is what the providers say in their own documents; we have not audited them.
privacy.s7P1: Your account and lists stay until you delete your account. Sign-in records (including the IP address and browser) stay until about a day after the sign-in expires (7 days after your last visit), or until you delete your account. One-time links stay up to 1 hour (password reset) or 10 minutes (Google sign-in) and are then removed by the daily clean-up. Request counters are kept for about a day at most. Record details from Discogs are kept for at most 6 hours.
privacy.s7P1GoogleOnly: Your account and lists stay until you delete your account. Sign-in records (including the IP address and browser) stay until about a day after the sign-in expires (7 days after your last visit), or until you delete your account. The one-time record of a Google sign-in stays up to 10 minutes and is then removed by the daily clean-up. Request counters are kept for about a day at most. Record details from Discogs are kept for at most 6 hours.
privacy.s7P2: Technical copies: our database provider (Neon) keeps a change history so the database can be restored; how long depends on the plan (hours on the free plan, up to days on paid plans), so deleted data can still exist there for that time. Brevo keeps delivery records of the emails it sent under its own settings. The operator may keep a short-lived private copy of the database (for example before a risky change) and deletes it soon after.
privacy.s7P2GoogleOnly: Technical copies: our database provider (Neon) keeps a change history so the database can be restored; how long depends on the plan (hours on the free plan, up to days on paid plans), so deleted data can still exist there for that time. The operator may keep a short-lived private copy of the database (for example before a risky change) and deletes it soon after.
privacy.s8Delete: Delete: Account > “Delete my account” removes your account, sessions and lists right away. Some technical copies disappear on their own: request counters within about a day, and provider logs and database history within the periods in “How long we keep it”.
privacy.s8Export: Export: Account > “Download my data” gives you your name, email, language, whether your email is verified, picture address (if you signed in with Google), sign-up date and lists as a file; your lists can also be exported as CSV or JSON from the lists page. The file does not include technical sign-in records (IP address, browser) or request counters; ask us if you want them.
privacy.s8Correct: Correct: you can change your language in Account. To change your name or email, use the contact page.
privacy.s8P1: You can ask us for a copy of your personal data, to correct it, to delete it, to restrict how we use it, to object to its use, and, where it applies, to receive the data you gave us in a common file format. Write to the contact address; we answer within one month (this can be extended for complex requests). You can also complain to the data protection authority of the country where you live or work (in Norway: Datatilsynet); in Ukraine you can complain to the Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights or to a court.
privacy.s9P1: Vinilium does not ask for or check your age and is not designed for children. If you are a parent and your child has an account, write to the contact address and we will delete it. [NEEDS LEGAL REVIEW] The minimum age we should set (it differs between countries) is not decided.
privacy.s10P1: Passwords are stored only as salted hashes (scrypt) that we cannot read. The site is served over HTTPS and the sign-in cookie cannot be read by scripts. We take reasonable care, but no system is perfectly secure.
privacy.s11P1: If this page changes in a way that matters, the date above changes too.
privacy.s11P2: If we change what we collect, why, who receives it or how you can use your rights, we will tell signed-in users by email or by a notice on the site before the change applies.
privacy.s2AccountGoogleOnly: Your account: your name, your email address, your language, the date you signed up and whether your email address is verified, the link to your Google account, and the name and picture address Google provides. We need your name and email address to create an account. We do not store Google’s access tokens. An account created earlier with a password still holds that password in hashed form, which we cannot read.
